title: KPMG Law US approved as an Arizona Alternative Business Structure — first Big Four firm licensed to practice law in the United States
pub: LawSites (Bob Ambrogi), 27 Feb 2025; Georgetown Journal of Legal Ethics blog (Connor O'Loughlin), 7 Apr 2025
author: Bob Ambrogi · Connor O'Loughlin

dom.t: Work redesign: Jagged capability demands selective deployment

st.t: Ownership reform: Investment openings may miss justice needs
st.an: The source advances Arizona’s ABS regime and KPMG’s commercial entry as evidence that ownership reform produces lower-cost, more accessible services while preserving ethics. This cuts against the cluster’s central caution that investment and market entry do not themselves demonstrate justice-gap reductions, particularly because KPMG targets corporate legal departments rather than unmet civil legal need.
qs: As demonstrated by KPMG, the ABS program has paved the way for greater access to legal services at a lower cost than law firms typically demand and technological developments that will increase the capabilities of lawyers worldwide.

However, Arizona’s ABS program demonstrates that by eliminating this rule, it is possible to promote public welfare by fostering innovation in the legal field while still maintaining the ethical standards that the rule was meant to protect.

st.t: Work redesign: Jagged capability demands selective deployment
st.an: The source provides a concrete provider-side example of work redesign: KPMG’s Arizona ABS would use playbooks and technology-enabled managed services to shift high-volume, form-driven contracting away from legal departments, allowing their lawyers to focus on core work. It materially extends the cluster through an operating-model and provider-boundary case, though its claimed benefits are prospective and it does not address verification or task-level performance evidence.
qs: - **Volume contracting**: Volume contract managed services will enable companies to design playbooks and technology-enabled solutions to handle high-volume contract obligations that currently burden legal departments.
We will be able to help relieve those burdens so legal departments and other legal advisors can focus on their core missions.

st.t: Workflow unbundling: Buyers challenge time-based production
st.an: The source accepts the workflow-unbundling logic and adds a concrete provider-side example: KPMG’s Arizona ABS plans to use technology-enabled managed services for standardised, high-volume contract work, allowing legal departments to concentrate on core matters. It materially develops the cluster’s claims about routine-work segmentation, scalable operating capability and alternative organisational structures, though its benefits remain prospective and it does not substantively address pricing, junior training or verification risks.
qs: - **Volume contracting**: Volume contract managed services will enable companies to design playbooks and technology-enabled solutions to handle high-volume contract obligations that currently burden legal departments.
We will be able to help relieve those burdens so legal departments and other legal advisors can focus on their core missions.

st.t: Big Four: Integration matters more than replacement
st.an: The source supports the cluster’s framing by documenting a selective regulatory opening in Arizona and KPMG’s plans for technology-enabled, scalable contracting services. It presents prospective capacity and integration with legal departments and advisers, not evidence of superior performance, nationwide liberalisation or inevitable law-firm replacement.
qs: - **Volume contracting**: Volume contract managed services will enable companies to design playbooks and technology-enabled solutions to handle high-volume contract obligations that currently burden legal departments.

st.t: Outside capital: Permission does not create investable firms
st.an: The source supports the synthesis’s qualified view: Arizona’s ABS regime enables capital-backed legal-service experimentation and KPMG plans technology reinvestment, but approval remains conditioned by conflicts controls, compliance audits and unresolved interstate constraints. Its claimed benefits are largely prospective rather than evidence of investability or improved outcomes.
qs: While law firms must spend massive amounts of capital on retaining their top attorneys, KPMG plans to reinvest its capital into technology, allowing it to enhance its capabilities across all of its services.[[46]](#_edn46)  KPMG Law US demonstrates the advantages of the ABS structure promoted by the Arizona Supreme Court.

kp.k: Arizona licenses the first Big Four US legal subsidiary
kp.d: Ambrogi reports that the Arizona Supreme Court approved KPMG Law US on February 27, 2025, following the ABS Committee’s January recommendation, making KPMG the first Big Four firm with a subsidiary licensed to practice law in the United States. KPMG says the subsidiary will be independently managed but strategically aligned with its Tax practice. This is a reported regulatory and organisational development, rather than evidence of subsequent service outcomes.
qs: KPMG LLP, the U.S. audit, tax, and advisory firm, became the first Big Four firm with a subsidiary licensed to practice law in the United States
KPMG Law US will operate as an independently managed subsidiary of KPMG LLP and maintain strategic alignment with the KPMG LLP Tax practice, the company said.

kp.k: Initial services target high-volume corporate legal processes
kp.d: KPMG’s FAQs, reproduced by Ambrogi, identify volume contracting, remediation, M&A contract harmonisation and legal managed services as the practice’s principal work. The proposed mechanism is technology-supported standardisation and scale, relieving corporate legal departments of repetitive contractual administration so they and their other advisers can focus on core priorities. These are planned services and claimed benefits, not measured productivity gains.
qs: KPMG Law US will primarily deliver large-scale, process-driven work, such as volume contracting, remediation exercises, M&A-driven harmonization of contracts, and other legal managed services.
Volume contract managed services will enable companies to design playbooks and technology-enabled solutions to handle high-volume contract obligations that currently burden legal departments.
We will be able to help relieve those burdens so legal departments and other legal advisors can focus on their core missions.

kp.k: Generative AI supports an integrated tax-and-legal platform
kp.d: KPMG presents AI and technology investments as enabling scalable legal services. Its Digital Gateway platform combines tax and legal data with analytics and reporting intended to support governance, risk management and actionable insights. The source provides corporate capability and benefit claims, rather than benchmarks, quantified savings or evidence of autonomous legal work.
qs: Digital Gateway serves as a control tower for a company’s suite of tax and legal data, providing advanced analytics and reporting capabilities, empowering tax and legal teams to enhance governance, manage risk and provide actionable insights.

By combining cutting-edge artificial intelligence and advanced technology solutions with legal services, we are proud to be a first mover with this capability and to offer the most holistic range of tech-enabled services in the marketplace for our clients’ evolving needs.

kp.k: Global capabilities underpin the proposed US expansion
kp.d: KPMG says its member firms have delivered legal services for more than a decade and operate in more than 80 jurisdictions, providing experience and capabilities for the US subsidiary. Ambrogi also reproduces a KPMG International statement reporting 10% Tax & Legal Services growth, attributed to several demand drivers including AI-enabled managed services and transformation; this is not a standalone measure of AI’s contribution or US subsidiary performance.
qs: Globally, KPMG member firms have delivered innovative legal services for more than a decade, now in more than 80 jurisdictions.
Tax & Legal Services grew by 10%, driven by client demand for our AI enabled managed service and transformation capability, our legal capability and assisting clients navigate global tax reform.

kp.k: Big Four entry combines competition and complementary specialisation
kp.d: O’Loughlin anticipates some competition with Big Law but reports KPMG’s positioning around specialised, high-volume post-merger integration rather than managing and closing major transactions. He reports KPMG’s expectation that extending existing accounting, tax and consulting capabilities can lower costs, and contrasts its intended technology reinvestment with large law firms’ expenditure on retaining attorneys. These are strategic expectations, not demonstrated displacement or comparative cost findings.
qs: While Big Law firms are still likely the most capable of managing and closing large M&A transactions, KPMG believes that it is well-suited to provide high-volume post-merger legal services such as integrating legal contracts and tech systems, tasks that typically overburden corporate legal departments.

While law firms must spend massive amounts of capital on retaining their top attorneys, KPMG plans to reinvest its capital into technology, allowing it to enhance its capabilities across all of its services.

kp.k: Ownership reform enables capital and multidisciplinary service delivery
kp.d: O’Loughlin reports that Arizona eliminated its own professional-conduct Rule 5.4 in 2020 and established an ABS framework effective January 1, 2021. He quotes the Arizona Supreme Court website’s rationales: technological innovation, additional capital, equity incentives for non-lawyer partners and combined legal/non-legal services. These are the reform’s stated rationales, distinct from changes to the ABA Model Rule or measured effects.
qs: Arizona Code of Judicial Administration (ACJA) § 7-209 was subsequently enacted to establish the regulatory framework of the ABS program, taking effect January 1, 2021.
It will allow for greater technological innovations in the delivery of legal services to the public.
It will provide additional capital to be infused in legal firms.
It will allow for “one-stop shops” to be able to provide legal and non-legal services to a client.

kp.k: Fee-sharing restrictions frame an independence-versus-innovation debate
kp.d: O’Loughlin reports competing arguments about Model Rule 5.4. Defenders see restrictions on non-lawyer ownership and fee sharing as protection against conflicting shareholder incentives and difficulties regulating non-lawyers. Critics argue that restrictions impede organisational growth, prevent cost and revenue synergies, sustain high prices and disadvantage law firms against affordable DIY legal software. These are reported normative and economic arguments, not empirical estimates.
qs: Model Rule 5.4 protects the lawyer from the pressures of having to serve the interests of both their clients and the shareholders of the business, which at times may be adverse.
Because of this, the judicial administration of a state’s ethics rules would be difficult in scenarios where an entity is owned and controlled by parties held to different ethical standards.

If lawyers and non-lawyers could share fees, they could benefit from the cost and revenue synergies generated by the combination of services provided, which would increase the competition among legal service providers and reduce the costs for legal services.

kp.k: ABS oversight retains professional obligations despite non-lawyer ownership
kp.d: O’Loughlin describes governance requirements protecting lawyers’ independence, client interests, confidentiality and work standards, alongside ownership disclosure, a required Arizona-licensed compliance lawyer, a code of conduct and biennial licence renewal. He reports that the Arizona State Bar initiated no complaints and no licensed ABS faced disciplinary action in the programme’s first three years; the reported observation concerns that period and those enforcement measures.
qs: Approved applicants must also renew their license every two years after the Committee reassesses whether the regulatory objectives and governance concerns continue to justify licensure.

The compliance lawyer is responsible for ensuring that all lawyers and authorized persons of the ABS comply with their ethical and professional responsibilities and the regulatory requirements of the ABS program.
In the first three years of the ABS program, the Arizona State Bar did not initiate any complaints nor was any disciplinary action taken against any licensed ABS.

kp.k: KPMG approval imposes audit-client exclusions and internal monitoring
kp.d: O’Loughlin reports specific conditions intended to address conflicts and maintain ethical standards: KPMG Law US cannot serve audit clients of KPMG or its member firms, although clients receiving other services remain eligible. Its compliance lawyer must also conduct semi-annual internal audits and report findings. These conditions qualify the proposed integrated-service model.
qs: Most importantly, KPMG Law US cannot provide legal services for any client that receives auditing services from KPMG or any of its member firms, but may still provide legal work to clients who receive services other than auditing.
Additionally, the KPMG Law US compliance lawyer is required to conduct semi-annual internal audits to ensure compliance with the ABS requirements and prepare a report of these findings.

kp.k: National reach remains conditional on each jurisdiction’s rules
kp.d: KPMG’s FAQs propose co-counsel, referral and staffing relationships to expand beyond Arizona, expressly subject to applicable legal and ethical rules. O’Loughlin highlights the difficulty posed by other jurisdictions’ fee-sharing restrictions and reports plans to avoid Arizona lawyers holding themselves out as licensed elsewhere. Arizona approval is therefore presented alongside jurisdiction-specific constraints, not unrestricted national authorisation.
qs: KPMG Law US will operate within each State’s ethics rules just like every other law firm.

We can co-counsel, refer or partner with separate staffing firms and other law firms, to expand services across jurisdictions, subject in all cases to legal and ethics rules in its various jurisdictions.
For these clients, KPMG plans to use staffing agencies and co-counseling relationships with other law firms, ensuring that no Arizona lawyer holds themselves out as a lawyer in another jurisdiction.

kp.k: Public-access benefits remain an argument rather than measured outcomes
kp.d: O’Loughlin links ABS reform to public welfare and greater access through lower-cost services, and concludes that KPMG illustrates innovation compatible with ethical standards. The document’s concrete KPMG service examples concern corporate legal processes; its broader access claims are authorial conclusions and reported reform arguments rather than findings measuring reduced unmet civil legal need. He recommends continually testing ethics rules against professional standards and public well-being.
qs: As a result, there would be greater access to legal services, as fees would no longer be cost-prohibitive and lawyers could begin to partner with low-cost legal service providers managed by non-lawyers.

This case serves as a reminder to all lawyers that the ethics rules, while important, should be constantly tested to ensure that they maintain professional standards in ways that most effectively promote the well-being of the legal profession and the public at large.

cl.s: Concrete claim or prediction about how AI changes legal services, the legal profession, or legal markets (or, for a cross-domain source, its own domain)

pts.k: KPMG predicts that combining AI, technology platforms and legal services will enable integrated, large-scale legal work; O’Loughlin describes a related shift toward technology-funded competition and collaboration with traditional law firms.
pts.d: In Ambrogi’s report, KPMG vice chair of tax Rema Serafi claims that AI and advanced technology position KPMG Law US to transform legal-service delivery. KPMG’s reproduced FAQs say its cloud-based, generative-AI-enabled Digital Gateway will unlock insights and improve quality through integrated tax and legal data, analytics and reporting. KPMG targets volume contracting, remediation and M&A contract harmonization, predicting better controls, more standardized outcomes and reduced administrative burdens. These are company claims, rather than independent findings by Ambrogi. Separately, O’Loughlin reports KPMG’s expectation that its existing capabilities and technology investment will enable lower-cost, specialized services alongside its accounting, tax and consulting work. He anticipates both competition with Big Law and a complementary role in high-volume post-merger work. The latter claims concern technology-enabled service delivery broadly, not effects isolated to AI.

cl.s: Evidence basis offered for the claim (data, benchmarks, cases, experience, authority, or none)

pts.k: The sources offer licensing documentation, company statements, existing network experience and aggregate business growth as context, rather than measured outcomes from KPMG Law US’s AI-enabled work.
pts.d: Ambrogi cites the February 27, 2025 Arizona Supreme Court approval order and reproduces KPMG’s statements and FAQs. KPMG supports its scaling ambitions by pointing to technology investments, more than a decade of global legal-services experience and operations in more than 80 jurisdictions. A quoted KPMG International press release reports 10% Tax & Legal Services growth, attributing it to several drivers including AI-enabled managed services and transformation; this is an aggregate company-reported result, not a measurement of AI’s separate contribution or of the new US subsidiary’s performance. O’Loughlin relies on Bloomberg reporting, regulatory provisions and Arizona judicial materials. His account of no initiated complaints or disciplinary action in the ABS program’s first three years supplies regulatory context, not evidence of AI accuracy or productivity. Neither document provides AI benchmarks, quantified US client savings or comparative task-performance results.

cl.s: Stated or implied timeframe, conditions or qualifications under which the claim holds

pts.k: The service-transformation claims are prospective from the 2025 licensing event, without a specified delivery or market-impact deadline, and depend on regulatory compliance and technology-enabled scaling.
pts.d: Ambrogi reports approval on February 27, 2025; O’Loughlin discusses its implications on April 7, 2025. KPMG describes services it will deliver and capabilities it intends to leverage, without forecasting a date or magnitude for savings or market displacement. Arizona’s ownership reforms enable the subsidiary’s entry, but its licence does not confer unrestricted nationwide practice rights. KPMG says expansion will use co-counsel, referrals and staffing or law-firm partnerships subject to each jurisdiction’s rules. O’Loughlin reports that KPMG Law US cannot serve audit clients of KPMG or its member firms and must undertake semi-annual internal compliance audits. These are conditions on the business model supporting the technology claims, not AI-specific performance conditions.

cl.s: Who is affected and how (market segment, role, firm type, clients, or the public)

pts.k: The immediate intended beneficiaries are corporate legal and tax teams; traditional law firms face specialized competition and partnership opportunities rather than a stated wholesale replacement.
pts.d: KPMG targets business clients whose legal departments handle repetitive, high-volume contracting and post-merger integration. Its predicted benefit is relief from process work so internal teams and other legal advisers can concentrate on core or strategic priorities. Tax and legal teams are also promised stronger governance, risk management and actionable data insights. O’Loughlin presents Big Law as likely to retain an advantage in managing and closing major M&A transactions while KPMG handles specialized downstream work. His broader conclusions connect ABS reform with public welfare and lower-cost access, but the concrete KPMG examples concern enterprise services, not demonstrated reductions in unmet civil legal need. Neither source predicts specific lawyer job losses, staffing ratios or autonomous replacement of lawyers.
